newsitem.title: ITALY: Business as usual in Venice on "independence day".
newsitem.headline: Business as usual in Venice on "independence day".

text.p: Venetians broadly turned their backs on Umberto Bossi's bid to split Italy on Sunday, concentrating on the far more profitable business of catering to the tourists.
Arrigo Cipriani, whose world-renowned Harry's Bar was serving up its usual Sunday lunches to the well-heeled, slammed the separatist leader as a madman.
"Unfortunately Mr Bossi's place should be in the mad house," the besuited restaurateur said over a drink at the bar.
"The lunatic asylums are full of Napoleons and the like and he is part of the family. That said, he's also a snob. He has shown that by choosing Venice for its image."
He added: "Venice has an image but of its own. Not for others".
Over in St Mark's Square, where hordes of tourists queued to get into the Basilica and tiptoed across the water-logged square, birdseed seller Sebastian Ohs was no happier.
"Personally, I think Bossi is a pain in the neck. We're trying to work here," he said sitting in front of his neatly arranged bags full of maize.
"The tourists are still here but a lot of those who usually come on a Sunday have been scared away because of the crowds."
A large Italian flag hung in the square between two flags depicting the golden-winged lion of Venice on a red background.
Valdo Tomatilli, a Socialist councillor from a nearby town, was in the square draped in the Italian flag as a protest against Bossi.
"This is to show that millions of people don't think like Bossi," he said, watched by bemused tourists. "At the beginning, Bossi was a good person but he has changed," Tomatilli said.

Flag-waving militants from all over northern Italy thronged the lagoon front in bright sunshine from St Mark's Square to the Piazza Dei Sette Martiri where Bossi was due to declare "independence" for his "Federal Republic of Padania".
Gondolier Roberto Vianello was watching the crowd go by.
"It has created a few problems for work today," he said. "But when something like the Pink Floyd concert happened a few years ago, it created more problems."
Directly opposite the grandstand erected for Bossi's declaration, an Italian flag fluttered from a window of a building inhabited mostly by the poor and elderly.
On the tiled roof of the building, three shirts -- green, white and red as the Italian flag -- were strategically hung out to dry on a washing line.
The flags infuriated green-shirted League officials and the mass of flag-waving faithful but they remained firmly in place.
Bossi's visit to Venice is the culmination of three days travelling along the Po river in a semi-mystical prelude to founding his new "northern state".
Another man carried a placard declaring "Christ is also with the people of Padania".
League officials, meanwhile, handed out pamphlets to inform tourists about what was going on.
John Jones, an engineer from the east side of Manhattan, was not over-excited by it all despite the discreet presence of riot police stationed nearby and in the back alleys.

"It's pretty mild compared to what I've seen in New York," he said. "I've never understood Italian politics, through all their governments and through all the years," said Jones, who comes to Italy on holidays every two years.
"Looking around at the people, I think it's just an excuse to have some fun."
